explanations.explanation: This feature responds to short directive or metadata phrases—imperative labels, form‐field instructions, and license/permission statements—that appear as headings or commands in technical, UI, and legal text.
This feature detects the sentence-final period that closes off a title or heading-style phrase.

This feature detects the “segment‐separator” punctuation in structured names—i.e. the dots in package/import paths, the slashes in file paths, and the colons (or dots) in XML namespaces or attribute names that delimit hierarchical identifiers.
This neuron is a detector for the period punctuation that marks the end of a declarative sentence (i.e. the sentence-final “.” in news‐style prose).

This neuron is basically a “continuation‐piece” detector – it fires on BPE tokens that don’t begin a new word (i.e. tokens without the space-marker hyphen).  In text you see it light up on internal subword pieces like “är” in Finnish pärjäävät, on the Romanian suffix “or” in lor, and even on tokens like “–” or “-” when they serve as internal hyphens or minus signs rather than standalone, word-initial symbols.
This feature detects the sentence-ending full stop (“.”) in English prose, marking the boundary at the end of diverse texts (scientific abstracts, news reports, tech write-ups, etc.).

This feature lights up on tokens that appear in top‐of‐file or top‐of‐document boilerplate/metadata sections—things like license‐exception markers (EXCEPT), “generated by” stamps (dump), section headings in legal captions (Ple. in Common Pleas), and accompanying license notes. In other words, it flags document‐level header or boilerplate markers.

1. Detects the phrase “shift work” in clinical/epidemiological study contexts, i.e. occupational-exposure discussion in medical research.  
2. Picks up the heading “Thoughts” as a blog or personal-reflection section title in a web UI.  
3. Fires on “Chris <Surname>” constructions referring to sports figures in news headlines or articles.  
4. Activates on “Matt” when used as the given name of a high-profile media personality.  
5. Marks sentence-initial “Hope” whether used as a friendly opener (“Hope you…”) or as the abstract noun in academic prose.  
6. Flags the UI label “Related Posts” in online articles as a content-recommendation heading.  
7. Responds to the imperative “Talk about…” in headings or calls-to-action within reviews or guides.  
8. Highlights “Jonathan” when used as an author byline or personal name in announcements.  
9. Picks up passive-voice headline patterns like “Evidence sought” in news stories.  
10. Detects the proper name “Jayamala,” i.e. Indian public-figure references.  
11. Marks narrative openings starting with “Ever since…” in both informal and promotional copy.  
12. Activates on two-word technical medical terms beginning with “psych… morbidity.”  
13. Fires on “Gary” when used as a first name in informal diagnostic or troubleshooting dialogue.  
14. Picks up the verb “urges” in news reporting, signaling public advisories or calls for action.

explanations.explanation: This neuron fires on high-level discourse cues—words that structure or qualify the flow of a statement (future/conditional markers like ’ll / will / if, enumerators like “firstly” / “three,” stance verbs “feel” / “look,” intensifiers “really,” fillers “yeah,” even brand‐name tags like “Roster”). In other words, it detects connective or modal tokens that organize discourse and signal speaker attitude.
This feature fires on the sentence‐ending period that closes a copyright or license attribution line in a source‐code header (e.g. the “.” after “Microsoft Corporation” or “Facebook, Inc”).

This feature is detecting the boilerplate header block of U.S. appellate‐court opinions—i.e. the structured metadata lines (court name and circuit/district, docket or “No.” numbers, the “v.” separator between parties, phrases like “AND NOW,” dates, judges, etc.).

This feature fires on the little word-parts that make up technical scientific terms—Latin/Greek roots and affixes (e.g. lip-, ethn-, poly-, phenyl-, –crystalline, –peritoneal, –genic, etc.) in biomedical, chemical and related jargon.

This feature lights up on the framing words used in formal/legal/technical texts to define a document’s scope, purpose or constraints—e.g. section-intro markers like “related,” “pertains,” “arises,” “seeks,” “limitations,” “reserved,” or “reviewed” that announce field-of-invention clauses, license limitations, court decisions, etc.

This neuron is basically a subword-n-gram detector: it fires on common 2–3-letter BPE pieces that correspond to high-frequency English affixes or morphemes (e.g. the superlative ending “-est,” corporate fragments like “com,” “or,” “con,” “dist,” “let,” “us,” etc.).

This feature picks out the little “boilerplate” labels and directives that sit in document preambles or headers—tokens that introduce structured metadata or operational clauses (e.g. import statements in code, policy keywords like “discourteous,” court‐heading ordinals like “FIFTH,” or annotation/library names like “Serializer”).

Ama – Marks the informal, emphatic exclamation “Amazing” (or its variants), signaling a strong positive reaction or surprise in conversational text.  
Ep – Identifies the scientific prefix “epigenetic,” flagging domain-specific discussions of epigenetic regulation and programming in biomedical literature.  
Social – Flags the standalone term “Social” when used as a classifier (e.g. “Social media,” “Social engineering,” “Social cohesion”), denoting topics about societal networks, behaviors, or community systems.

explanations.explanation: This neuron is a subword‐fragment detector: it fires on those 2–4-letter BPE pieces that frequently sit inside names (Steffy, Tebow, Aaron, Sanabria, McNabb) and technical terms (microrobots, chalcogel, nocturia, Atmospheres). In other words, it marks common interior subword chunks of proper nouns and specialized vocabulary.

This neuron is essentially a “lead‐word” detector—it lights up on the first salient content word (main verb or head noun/adjective) in a new section, title or opening sentence. It flags the key action or topic that launches a headline, post or paragraph.

This feature flags the little formatting and discourse-marking tokens people slip into online posts and comments—horizontal-rule lines (“======”, “~~~”, “–––”) and short cue words (“please”, “helpful”, “this”, suffixes like “esy” in “Courtesy”) that signal section breaks, polite requests or comment/meta transitions in forum/blog threads.

This feature detects domain-specific scientific entities—especially technical nouns in biomedical and physical‐science texts such as enzyme names (–ase), ligands/agonists, cell types, molecular species (anions, proteins), organisms, physical phenomena (stars, plasmons), etc.

This neuron flags the kind of boilerplate‐style qualifiers and introductory tokens you see in headers/about sections—greeting verbs (“visiting”), attribute adjectives/adverbs (“multidisciplinary,” “established,” “official,” “talented,” “really”), dates/locations (“1997,” “Missouri,” “USA”)—that commonly occur in site welcome messages, product or company intros, academic abstracts and professional bios.

This feature specializes in spotting boundary‐marking punctuation in formal or technical prose—most often commas that follow descriptive modifiers (adjectives or past-participles like “granted,,” “published,,” “severe,,” “smooth,,” “simple,,” “susceptible,,” etc.) and hyphens in compound qualifiers (e.g. “last-16”). In effect, it flags the punctuation that separates or closes off a modifier or clause.

This feature detects the syntactic markers that introduce new user-defined types or declarations across languages—tokens like “type,” “struct,” “class,” “interface,” “dictionary,” “#ifndef,” etc., which signal the start of a type/struct/class/interface/macro definition.

This head is basically a little “morpheme‐ending” detector – it lights up on the BPE subtokens that carry English inflectional or derivational endings (the ‑ing gerund/participle, the ‑ed/-ated past‐participle, the ‑er comparative, etc.).

This neuron flags discourse markers that introduce framed or subordinate clauses—especially hypotheticals, conditions, examples or indirect questions.  It lights up on words like “Suppose,” “if/what if,” “when,” “for example,” “whether,” “that” or “Let me,” all of which set up a scenario, condition, example or embedded question.

This feature fires on the first sub‐token of a hyphenated (or similarly punctuated) compound, effectively marking the boundary and start of the second element in multi‐part words across scientific, technical or colloquial contexts.

The feature is a “relationship‐linker” detector: it fires on small function words—chiefly the preposition “of” (and its cousins like “for” or “to”)—when they join parts of multiword proper names or institutional titles (e.g. “Helen of Troy,” “Royal College of…,” “Organisation for Economic…”).

This feature detects “add-on” markers—tokens that signal continuation or enumeration—whether in running prose (additive conjunctions like Romanian și or English and/Both/Again), headings or section labels (REVIEW, AUDIO), punctuation that links clauses (., “”), or structural cues in code (indentation, docstrings/triple-quotes, list/bullet markers).
This feature responds to cardinal‐number mentions—whether spelled out or in digits—marking tokens that express numeric quantities (ages, counts, years, percentages, etc.) across contexts.

This neuron fires on “signpost” words that announce a new topic or section in technical/formal text—whether it’s a problem label in code Q&As (“error,” “problem,” “=”), a document header or role in legal opinions (“Memorandum Opinion,” “Plaintiff,” “Appellant,” court names), or methodological terms in science (“calculations,” “models,” “measurements”). It marks the lexical cues that introduce the main issue, section heading, or method across diverse technical domains.

This neuron detects formal, domain-specific “procedure” keywords that mark methods or rules in structured prose—e.g. database names (MEDLINE), experimental labels (in vitro/in vivo), analytic verbs and qualifiers (measured, stratified, multidimensional, white matter) and legal directives (prohibits, only).

explanations.explanation: This neuron seems to be a “line-start/heading” detector – it spikes on the very first token of a headline or list entry (whether that’s a capitalized word like “All” or “The,” a date numeral plus comma, a leading dash or “@,” etc.), marking the beginning of a new segment.

This feature detects the interrogative determiner “Which” when it opens a question—i.e. sentences asking the reader to choose among alternatives (across domains like cat breeds, planets, credit scores, math problems, etc.).

This neuron is basically a “continuation‐subword” detector: it lights up on the little 2–4-letter BPE fragments that occur as interior pieces of larger (often all-caps) words in headlines, titles or legal headers (e.g. “ID” in FRIDAY, “OCK” in SHOCKING, “PART” in DEPARTMENT, “UT” in MUTUAL, etc.).
